items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom — GS Positioning Reset
items.title: Goldman (Mueller-Glissmann): positioning reset improves asymmetry — but 'this isn't capitulation'
items.idea: GS argues the latest liquidation pushed sentiment and positioning toward levels historically associated with better forward equity returns, but the most convincing contrarian signals (true capitulation) are still missing. Investors are carrying materially less risk than a few weeks ago, which tilts upside/downside more favourably without removing the original risks.
items.angle: Asymmetry-improved-but-no-capitulation is the classic setup for a choppy, two-way tape: good for selling vol into squeezes, bad for directional size. Pairs with Krinsky's March-lows warning below.
items.tweetA: Goldman says positioning is cleaner but nobody has actually thrown in the towel. That's the worst of both worlds for a bear and a bull: no forced sellers left to squeeze lower, no washed-out crowd to fuel a real rally. Range trade until something breaks.
items.tweetB: The tell I'm watching isn't sentiment surveys, it's whether systematic deleveraging is done. CTAs and HFs cut, retail bought. If the next leg down comes, the people holding the bag this time aren't the levered ones. $SPY $QQQ

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom — GS Positioning Reset
items.title: Hedge funds and systematics de-grossing aggressively while retail buys the dip — a widening divergence
items.idea: Per the GS note, hedge funds and systematic investors have cut exposure aggressively while retail has moved in the opposite direction. GS flags the divergence as potentially decisive for the next sustained move.
items.angle: Retail-vs-pro divergence after a liquidation historically resolves in favour of whoever has dry powder — here that's the pros. Watch retail flow data next week for exhaustion.
items.tweetA: Pros sold, retail bought. Every bottom story needs someone to be the last seller. If it's retail, that's still ahead of us.
items.tweetB: Hidden signal in the Goldman note: the de-risking has already happened in the levered books. Retail now owns the float. That makes the next drawdown less violent but slower — death by grind, not by margin call.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom — GS Positioning Reset
items.title: Repositioning has spread beyond equities: tech options, currencies and gold all reset
items.idea: GS notes the repositioning extended past stocks into technology options, FX and gold, creating 'a more interesting investment landscape' even as the drivers of the correction remain in place.
items.angle: Cross-asset reset means hedges are cheaper/cleaner than two weeks ago. Gold getting thrown overboard in a margin call (Dark Side's gold primer yesterday) is the same liquidation in another asset.
items.tweetA: When gold gets sold alongside semis, that's not a view on gold — it's a margin call. Cleaner gold positioning into a Fed that's about to hike again is an interesting setup. $GLD
items.tweetB: Tech call skew got crushed, then repriced on the Jensen squeeze. If GS is right that positioning is cleaner across assets, the cheapest hedge right now might be the one nobody sold: duration. $TLT

items.source: Bespoke Investment Group
items.title: Q3 GDP revised up 0.9pp to 4.3% — but trade shaved >3pp off growth
items.idea: Second Q3 GDP revision lifted real growth 0.9pp to 4.3%, yet net trade still subtracted more than three percentage points. Bespoke uses this to argue the 'AI is the whole economy' narrative is 'straightforwardly wrong'.
items.angle: A 4.3% print with a 3pp trade drag means domestic demand ran ~7%. That's hike territory, which is exactly what fed funds futures price for Dec 9 (Authers).
items.tweetA: 4.3% GDP with trade subtracting 3+ points. Back that out and US domestic demand ran near 7% annualized. And people want the Fed to pivot because the Nasdaq is down?
items.tweetB: The tariff reimposition on the EU and China lands right after a quarter where trade was already a 3pp drag. Either import front-running reverses into a GDP tailwind in Q4, or this is the new structural hole. Your Q4 nowcast depends on which.

items.source: Bespoke Investment Group
items.title: AI-related GDP categories surged to ~5% of GDP — yet consumption, not AI, still drives the economy
items.idea: Bespoke shows AI-related spending categories have climbed to about 5% of GDP, a huge surge, but argues consumption remains the dominant growth engine — the rest is paywalled.
items.angle: 5% of GDP is roughly the peak share of 1990s telecom/IT investment. The comparison matters more than whether AI 'drives' growth.
items.tweetA: AI capex at ~5% of GDP. Late-90s IT investment peaked around the same share. Not a prediction — just the historical altitude at which these booms got financed by credit instead of cash flow.
items.tweetB: Bespoke's Thanksgiving argument: AI isn't the whole economy. Fair. But it's the marginal economy — the part that swings. 5% of GDP doing 30%+ of the growth delta is still the thing the Fed and the bond market are reacting to.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom — AI Credit Boom Hits a Wall
items.title: US chip curbs freeze Southeast Asia data center lending — $49B APAC DC loan book suddenly carries Washington risk
items.idea: Asia-Pacific data center lending went from ~zero in 2023 to >$49B (Bloomberg). New US rules require licences for advanced AI chip purchases in Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil, plus extra licensing within 90 days for DCs leasing significant capacity to Chinese customers. The risk is no longer 'can the customer pay' but 'can the customer legally keep buying the service'.
items.angle: This is the credit transmission of export controls — the equity market celebrated Jensen, credit committees are repricing. Watch SEA DC REITs, regional banks and GPU-ABS spreads.
items.tweetA: $49B of APAC data center loans written on one assumption: Chinese hyperscalers can keep renting US silicon offshore. Washington just put a 90-day licence clock on that assumption. That's not a demand shock, it's a collateral shock.
items.tweetB: The equity market priced Jensen's return in a day. The loan market is pricing Washington's chip rule over 90 days. Guess which one tells you more about 2027 capex. $NVDA $SMCI

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom — AI Credit Boom Hits a Wall
items.title: Deal-by-deal: Bain's Bridge DC $6.6B, Digital Halo $372M, Aolani $480M, GMI Cloud $300M all stalled
items.idea: Lenders delayed Bain Capital-backed Bridge Data Centres' expanded $6.6B loan pending diligence on Malaysian sites serving ByteDance. A bank walked from Partners Group-backed Digital Halo's fully underwritten $372M loan (Alibaba customer). Aolani ($480M, ByteDance ties) is being reassessed; a private credit fund dropped out of GMI Cloud's $300M GPU loan for a Thai DC serving Tencent.
items.angle: The common factor is end-customer = Chinese hyperscaler. Geographic diversification across Malaysia/Singapore/Thailand gave zero protection because the risk is the customer's licence, not the country.
items.tweetA: Four deals, four countries' worth of 'diversification', one end-customer type: ByteDance, Alibaba, Tencent. Turns out the risk factor was never Malaysia. It was who's renting the racks.
items.tweetB: A bank walked away from a FULLY UNDERWRITTEN $372M loan. That's the line I'd underline. Underwriting risk you can price; a lender eating reputational cost to exit tells you the risk is unpriceable for now.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom — AI Credit Boom Hits a Wall
items.title: Citi, StanChart and Singapore banks reviewing DC books; UOB's ~$1B SRT getting harder to place
items.idea: More than a dozen regional bankers say teams are waiting for clarity. Citigroup, Standard Chartered and major Singaporean banks have begun broader DC exposure reviews. UOB is seeking a ~$1B significant risk transfer covering data center and infrastructure loans, but uncertainty is making it harder to complete. S&P (Nov 24) warned even a reversal of the rules may not restore confidence.
items.angle: SRT difficulty is the plumbing signal: when banks can't distribute risk, they stop originating. That's how a policy change becomes a credit cycle without a single default.
items.tweetA: Lending markets don't need defaults to tighten. They need banks that can't sell down what they already hold. UOB trying to offload ~$1B of DC risk and struggling is that moment, in miniature.
items.tweetB: S&P's point is the real one: even if Washington reverses, the lesson is learned. Policy risk is now permanently in the spread for any DC whose tenant list starts with a Chinese hyperscaler.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom — AI Credit Boom Hits a Wall
items.title: DayOne pulls US IPO; BlackRock consortium may cut bid for APAC DC portfolio
items.idea: DayOne Data Centers, whose largest customer is ByteDance, has put its US listing on hold. A BlackRock-involved consortium is considering lowering its offer for an Asia-Pacific data center portfolio. Valuations, not just credit availability, are being reassessed.
items.angle: When equity exits close and buyers chisel bids, the refinancing assumptions in the original loans break too. Read-across to any DC developer with China-tenant concentration.
items.tweetA: DayOne shelving its IPO is the equity-side confirmation of what credit already said. ByteDance as anchor tenant went from 'blue-chip offtake' to 'licence-dependent counterparty' in two weeks.
items.tweetB: Question nobody's asking: if Chinese AI demand can't rent offshore compute, where does it go? Onshore, on domestic chips. Bearish SEA DC developers, structurally bullish Huawei Ascend volume.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom — AI Credit Boom Hits a Wall
items.title: The 2022 Biden curbs built Southeast Asia's offshore-China compute ecosystem; the 2026 rules are dismantling its financing model
items.idea: Restrictions on advanced chip exports to China in 2022 incentivized an offshore computing ecosystem in Malaysia and Singapore (and increasingly Thailand/Indonesia), letting Chinese tech access high-end hardware outside the mainland. Banks financed it against recognizable customers and long contracts. The new licence regime targets exactly that workaround.
items.angle: Policy created the asset class; policy is now repricing it. A clean case study of regulatory reflexivity for anyone financing infra on top of a geopolitical arbitrage.
items.tweetA: Washington spent 2022 creating the Malaysian data center boom by accident, and 2026 un-creating it on purpose. If your investment thesis is a regulatory loophole, your exit is a press release.
items.tweetB: Johor's power grid, water, and land got allocated to ByteDance-adjacent compute. If that demand gets licensed away, who absorbs the stranded megawatts? Watch whether US hyperscalers quietly pick them up at a discount.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom — AI Credit Boom Hits a Wall
items.title: GPU-backed private credit is the most exposed layer: collateral value depends on who's legally allowed to use it
items.idea: Unlike property-backed DC lending, GPU financing rests on hardware whose usefulness, resale value and revenue depend on rapidly evolving tech and commercial deployability. If regulation restricts which customers can use it, the lender's collateral value becomes far murkier. Author expects higher required returns and tighter terms to become more permanent.
items.angle: GPU ABS and neocloud lenders were already wrestling with depreciation curves; now add a jurisdictional haircut. Watch CoreWeave-style spreads and neocloud refinancing.
items.tweetA: A GPU is collateral only if someone is allowed to rent it. Private credit priced H100s like aircraft. Turns out they're more like export-licensed weapons systems.
items.tweetB: Two haircuts on GPU collateral now: tech obsolescence (Blackwell → Rubin) and legal obsolescence (licence revoked). The first you can model. The second turns a 3-year depreciation schedule into a binary.

items.source: Bloomberg Points of Return / John Authers
items.title: Q3 GDP >4% annualized and supercore PCE above Fed tolerance — a Dec 9 hike priced as a near-certainty
items.idea: Q3 GDP grew at one of its best rates in three decades (Authers cites 4.2%), and PCE supercore (services ex-housing) confirmed CPI — above the Fed's zone of tolerance, contradicting the 'stickiness is just oil' argument. Fed funds futures price a December hike as virtually certain and now >2 hikes next year (vs one right after the midterms, but fewer than at September's rates scare).
items.angle: Supercore ignoring oil kills the 'transitory energy' dove case. Market wants a Powell-2018-style pivot; data argues the opposite.
items.tweetA: Supercore doesn't care about oil. It's above tolerance anyway. So the 'Fed is hiking into falling oil' argument has it backwards: the Fed is hiking into services inflation that oil never caused.
items.tweetB: Futures went from 1 hike after the midterms to 2+ now, in a few weeks, while the Nasdaq fell. Rates are repricing hawkish INTO an equity drawdown. That's the regime where the Fed put is struck far below spot.

items.source: Bloomberg Points of Return / John Authers
items.title: Robin Brooks: 'Markets heading for full meltdown' as Fed hikes into falling oil — blackout starts Saturday
items.idea: Brooks (Brookings) argues the Fed hiking into falling oil prices is a policy error supercharging real rates; with the pre-Dec 9 blackout beginning Saturday and no dovish pivot, 'the wheels might really start coming off' — possibly ending in no hike as markets melt down. Wednesday's reversal (gold and BTC dove then closed up, 10y dipped to 4.80% then 4.86%) weakened the argument somewhat.
items.angle: Blackout window = no Fed-speak backstop for ~10 days. That's a defined vol window into Dec 9.
items.tweetA: Fed blackout starts Saturday. That's ten days where nobody on the FOMC can talk the market off the ledge. If you're long vol, this is the cleanest calendar catalyst you'll get all year. $VIX
items.tweetB: Brooks says meltdown forces 'no hike'. Authers' data says supercore forces a hike. Somebody is about to be very wrong on Dec 9, and the options market is pricing it like a coin flip it isn't.

items.title: SOX still -17% since Huang's dismissal (-22% at Wednesday's low) — the 'Huang put' didn't restore the trend
items.idea: Despite the rebound, the SOX remains 17% below where it was when news of Huang's initial dismissal broke, and hit -22% at Wednesday's worst. Nvidia's travails 'stretch far beyond the soap opera around its CEO'.
items.angle: If the CEO return was the put and it couldn't hold, the issue is fundamentals/financing, not governance. Ties to the Asia credit story and Nvidia's credit cracks (Dark Side earlier).
items.tweetA: The market got the best possible governance outcome — Jensen back — and SOX is still down 17%. When the good news is fully delivered and the stock can't hold, the problem was never the CEO. $NVDA $SOXX
items.tweetB: Dark Side: Asian banks freezing DC loans over chip curbs. Authers: SOX can't recover even with Jensen back. Same story from two angles: the binding constraint moved from silicon supply to financing permission.

items.source: Bloomberg Points of Return / John Authers
items.title: The four-year 'long tech / short duration' trade has had only two interruptions — this is the third
items.idea: Authers: the dominant trade since ~2022 has been buying tech and selling long bonds. Only two significant interruptions before now. Huang's reinstatement was meant to be the 'put' drawing a line under this third break — the trend hasn't been regained, unlike after March's Iran peace feelers or Trump's Liberation Day tariff pause. Since September's 'bondpocalypse' (10y >5.25%), 'certainties have been shattered'.
items.angle: If long-tech/short-duration is broken, the pair flips: long duration as the hedge comes back. Positioning in that pair is enormous.
items.tweetA: The most crowded macro trade of the decade is long Nasdaq, short TLT. It has broken twice before and snapped back. This time the 'put' (Jensen) was delivered and it still didn't snap back. That's new. $QQQ $TLT
items.tweetB: 10y hit 5.25% in September and the tech trade survived. 10y at 4.86% now and tech is breaking. It was never about the level of yields — it was about whether earnings growth could outrun them.

items.source: Bloomberg Points of Return / John Authers
items.title: Nasdaq 100 forward P/E 'very, very cheap' vs trailing — the selloff only makes sense if estimates are wrong
items.idea: Tech earnings estimates have stopped accelerating but aren't yet falling. The gap between trailing and forward Nasdaq 100 P/E implies the market doubts forecasts. About two months until the next earnings download; if companies don't guide lower in coming weeks, valuations should tempt buyers.
items.angle: This is a falsifiable setup: watch pre-announcements and sell-side revisions in December. No cuts = buy signal.
items.tweetA: Forward P/E on the Nasdaq 100 is screaming cheap vs trailing. That gap is the market saying 'we don't believe your 2027 numbers'. Either estimates fall in December, or this is the buy of the year. No third option.
items.tweetB: The math: if forward multiple is way below trailing, the market's pricing an earnings cut that analysts haven't made. Watch December pre-announcements. Silence from the companies is bullish.

items.source: Bloomberg Points of Return / John Authers
items.title: Bowers: 'We need to see it's 2008, not 2000' — and Watling calls it a mid-cycle correction
items.idea: David Bowers (Absolute Strategy) argues strong earnings are inflationary via margins and a falling Nasdaq won't stop a tightening Fed; the Fed hiked through the 2000 bust and only cut to zero in 2008. Financing structures around AI remain 'opaque and circular, with Nvidia as a critical linchpin'. Chris Watling (Longview) calls November 'typical for a mid-cycle correction', and says a resolute Fed lets 10y yields fall.
items.angle: The Fed put is struck at 'financial crisis', not 'equity correction'. Opaque AI financing (Asia DC loans, Nvidia vendor financing) is the channel through which 2000 could become 2008.
items.tweetA: Bowers' frame: the Fed bails out 2008, not 2000. So the bull case for a pivot requires the AI financing web to actually break. Be careful what you're rooting for.
items.tweetB: Interesting split: Bowers sees a Fed that won't blink; Watling sees that same resolute Fed as what lets 10y yields fall. Hawkish Fed → lower long yields → bull steepener reversed. Duration might be the trade of the hike.

items.source: Bloomberg Points of Return / John Authers
items.title: US reimposed tariffs on the EU, China and others
items.idea: Authers' Points of Return lists the US reimposing tariffs on the EU, China and others among the day's developments, alongside the GDP/PCE data. Bloomberg Opinion also runs 'Chips and Rare Earths Keep the US-China Truce Fragile' (Mukherjee) and 'The Pentagon's NATO 3.0 Makes Only Russia Happy' (Kluth).
items.angle: Tariff reimposition after a quarter with a 3pp trade drag (Bespoke) adds goods-inflation pressure into a hiking Fed. Bad mix for multiples.
items.tweetA: Tariffs back on the EU and China, the same week supercore is above tolerance and the Fed is priced to hike. The 2018 playbook was tariffs + Fed pivot. 2026 is tariffs + Fed hike. Different ending.
items.tweetB: Chips, rare earths, tariffs, export licences for Malaysian data centers. The US-China 'truce' is being renegotiated one SKU at a time, and markets keep pricing each piece as isolated.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom — Cold Turkey (BTIG Krinsky)
items.title: Krinsky's 12-case study: NDX -5% then +5% the next day → avg -5.4% over 3 sessions, 11 of 12 down. Futures did exactly that.
items.idea: BTIG's Jonathan Krinsky found 12 occasions since 1985 where the Nasdaq 100 fell ≥5% in a session and rebounded ≥5% the next. Average and median return over the following three sessions: about -5.4%, with 11 of 12 negative. By Wednesday morning, Nasdaq futures implied almost exactly a 5.4% reversal from Monday's close.
items.angle: Small sample, but the forecast landed. If 11/12 holds, the follow-through question is what happens after the -5.4% — Krinsky's next warning is the March lows.
items.tweetA: 12 times since 1985 the Nasdaq dropped 5% and ripped 5% the next day. 11 of them were lower 3 sessions later, avg -5.4%. Wednesday morning futures were down... 5.4%. Back-to-back 5% days aren't strength. They're a market with no bid depth. $QQQ
items.tweetB: The question isn't whether Krinsky's study worked — it did. It's what a 5%-up day on a CEO rehiring tells you about liquidity. When one headline moves $2T, the market isn't pricing fundamentals, it's pricing who's forced.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom — Cold Turkey (BTIG Krinsky)
items.title: Krinsky's map: bearish at Oct 6 peak → 7,000 target → 7,250-7,350 rebound zone → now warns March lows may be next
items.idea: Krinsky turned bearish around the Oct 6 S&P peak, flagged breadth deterioration while indices held, targeted ~7,000 on the S&P, then called 7,250–7,350 as the tactical rebound zone and advised trimming near 7,300. The paywalled 'more uncomfortable' warning: the real capitulation may still be ahead, with March lows in play. Defensives outperforming and the dollar not confirming the rebound.
items.angle: A technician with this hit rate pointing to the March lows is a concrete downside anchor for hedging. Dollar non-confirmation is the cross-asset tell to watch.
items.tweetA: S&P 7,300 was the 'sell the rip' level and it was. Next stop on the same map: the March lows. When a strategist has been right on the top, the target, and the bounce, I'd at least size hedges to his next number.
items.tweetB: Under the hood the S&P 'equal weight' is holding up while tech bleeds. That sounds healthy. Historically it's what late-stage leadership failure looks like before the rest catches down. Defensives leading + dollar not confirming = not a bottom yet. $RSP $XLU

items.source: AI-RTZ #1282 / Michael Parekh
items.title: Anthropic vs OpenAI scoreboard: $81B vs ~$70B run rate, $895B vs ~$750B compute commitments, ~$1.2T vs $1.25T value
items.idea: Anthropic's annualized revenue run rate hit $81B (Oct 31, +$10B in a month); OpenAI heads to ~$70B exit pace. Compute commitments: ~$895B (Anthropic, up >$375B since the earlier $517B tally) vs ~$750B through 2030 (OpenAI). Value: OpenAI's last private round $1.25T pre-money (below the $1.4T sought); Anthropic ~$1.2T on traded shares this week.
items.angle: Both labs carry compute commitments ~10x their revenue run rate. That's the number that links AI equity to the credit stress in Asia DC lending.
items.tweetA: $81B revenue run rate, $895B compute committed. That's ~11 years of current revenue pre-spent on compute. Any company outside AI with that ratio gets called a leveraged bet. $ANT
items.tweetB: Coke and Pepsi flipped: Anthropic now out-earns OpenAI on revenue and out-commits it on compute. But both trade at roughly the same $1.2T. The market isn't paying for the revenue lead — it's pricing them as one trade.

items.source: AI-RTZ #1282 / Michael Parekh
items.title: OpenAI's Pachocki publishes internal 'perplexity' curve: loss fell ~5x more in 2026 than in the prior three years
items.idea: Chief scientist Jakub Pachocki's 'Perplexity and Intelligence' (Nov 22) shows OpenAI's internal base-model loss since GPT-3.5. Emergent capabilities mapped to thresholds: below ~0.8 came cybersecurity expertise and breakthrough math. GPT-6.2 Astra sits ~0.76; the unreleased internal model ~0.73. The base model barely moved from late 2023 through 2025, then the score fell ~5x as much in under a year. Next window (~0.68–0.70) expected to unlock capabilities nobody can name yet.
items.angle: A flat base model in 2024–25 coincided with the 'scaling wall' narrative; the 2026 drop is the rebuttal. That matters for whether compute commitments are rational.
items.tweetA: OpenAI's own chart: base-model progress was basically flat from late 2023 to 2025, then fell 5x faster in 2026. The 'scaling is dead' crowd was looking at exactly the window where it paused. $NVDA
items.tweetB: Pachocki says the next rung (0.68–0.70) unlocks capabilities 'nobody can name yet' and labs may not even be testing for them. That's the chief scientist telling you the eval regime is behind the model. Regulators should read that line twice.

items.source: AI-RTZ #1282 / Michael Parekh
items.title: Pachocki proposes an industry-wide 'first limit on development' measured by perplexity
items.idea: OpenAI's chief scientist proposes frontier labs agree on common limits (by perplexity and other metrics) they won't cross until humans can better understand and monitor AI — e.g. a successor to chain-of-thought monitors. He expects alignment auditing to degrade and models to grow more evaluation-aware. Anthropic's RSP v3 uses capability evals/ASL levels instead; no public Anthropic response yet.
items.angle: A voluntary cap measured by a metric each lab computes on its own data is unverifiable. Watch whether this becomes the template for regulators (EU AI Act compute thresholds, US).
items.tweetA: OpenAI wants a shared 'speed limit' measured in perplexity. Small problem: Pachocki himself says perplexity doesn't compare across labs. A speed limit where every car brings its own speedometer.
items.tweetB: The leapfrog problem: lead changed hands ~7 times in a year. Nobody slows down first. A self-imposed brake only works if it's coordinated — which in any other industry is called a cartel. Antitrust will have opinions.

items.source: AI-RTZ #1282 / Michael Parekh
items.title: Epoch Capabilities Index: Fable 5.2 and GPT-6.2 Astra tied at ~174, same $8/$40 per M tokens list price
items.idea: On Epoch AI's ECI, Anthropic's Fable 5.2 set a record Nov 9; GPT-6.2 Astra tied it eight days later at ~174. Both list at $8/M input and $40/M output. Since late 2025 the labs have leapfrogged about seven times. METR's time horizon is doubling roughly every 3.5 months and is getting hard to measure as tests saturate.
items.angle: Identical frontier pricing + capability parity = competition shifts to distribution, enterprise lock-in and cost of compute. Margin pressure ahead.
items.tweetA: Two trillion-dollar labs, same benchmark score, same price to the cent. When the product is identical, the winner is whoever has the cheaper cost of compute. That's a power and silicon story, not a model story.
items.tweetB: METR task horizon doubling every 3.5 months = ~10x every year. If that holds through 2027, the 'agent can do a week of human work' threshold arrives before most enterprises finish their AI pilots.

items.source: AI-RTZ #1282 / Michael Parekh
items.title: Claude went from leading <1% of Anthropic's AI research tasks in February to >25% by August
items.idea: Per Axios, cited by Parekh: Claude's share of Anthropic's AI research tasks it led rose from under 1% to over a quarter between February and August, while METR finds models advancing at nearly twice their historical pace. OpenAI says its latest models already make meaningful design contributions, and both labs are using AI to design AI chips.
items.angle: Recursive self-improvement is now a measured ratio, not a thought experiment. It's the cleanest explanation for the 2026 perplexity cliff.
items.tweetA: <1% to >25% in six months. That's the share of Anthropic's own AI research led by Claude. If the next six months do the same, the labs' biggest R&D input isn't people — it's their own compute bill.
items.tweetB: Why compute commitments of ~$900B might be rational: if models do a quarter of the research, GPU-hours become labour. You're not buying infrastructure, you're hiring researchers who never sleep.

items.source: AI-RTZ #1282 / Michael Parekh
items.title: Anthropic IPO round trip: $83 pricing → $111.50 open (~$2T) → now trading just under IPO price (~$1.2T)
items.idea: Anthropic priced Nov 18 at $83 (above range), raising $93.5B ($119.5B incl. Google/Microsoft/Nvidia/AMD private placement) — the biggest IPO ever, topping SpaceX in June. Opened $111.50 (~$2T), closed day one $97.17 (~$1.76T FD), has slipped every day since and this week traded just under $83. Q3 revenue ~$17B (+~12x YoY); >11,900 customers pay $100K+/yr; Q2 op profit ~$1B, Q3 small op loss. OpenAI lost ~$11B operating in Q3.
items.angle: Biggest-ever IPO breaking issue in a week during an AI-credit wobble = lockup and index-inclusion flows are the next catalysts. Also weighs on OpenAI's 2027 IPO timing.
items.tweetA: Anthropic: $2T at the open, below IPO price a week later. 12x revenue growth, and it still broke issue. That's not a verdict on Anthropic — it's what $119B of new supply does to a market already short on liquidity.
items.tweetB: OpenAI wanted $1.4T, raised at $1.25T. Anthropic opened at $2T, now ~$1.2T. The private and public marks just converged — downward. Every AI late-stage VC book is about to get re-marked off that number.

items.title: Pricing strategy split: Anthropic leans premium/margins, OpenAI cuts harder for usage; Anthropic mid-tier subs ~5x the value (SemiAnalysis)
items.idea: Parekh's 2026 pricing timeline shows Anthropic leaning on premium pricing and margins, OpenAI cutting prices harder to win usage. On subscriptions, SemiAnalysis estimates Anthropic's mid-tier plans offer about five times OpenAI's value. SpaceX (now home to xAI) IPO'd in June and may merge with Tesla next year — the 'third leg' of the trillion-dollar AI stool.
items.angle: If Anthropic is both premium on API and 5x value on subscriptions, it's subsidizing consumer to win enterprise — a margin question for the public stock.
items.tweetA: Anthropic charges premium on the API and gives away ~5x more on subscriptions than OpenAI. That's not a pricing strategy, it's a land grab funded by enterprise margins. Public shareholders will ask about that mix by Q1.
items.tweetB: Third trillion-dollar AI leg: SpaceX/xAI, possibly merging with Tesla next year. If that happens, $TSLA holders become xAI holders overnight. Index weight math on that merger would be wild.
